turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I came in because... things at work are getting a bit difficult. I'm a supervisor, retail, so I have to explain things to the team, like the inventory numbers or just getting the weekend schedule sorted out. But lately, when I try to do that, my words just start jumping all over the place. 

Like, I’ll start talking about the delivery trucks, which usually come on Thursdays. Thursday is actually when we do the big community dinner, and the church grill is still acting up—I was looking at the propane line just the other day and telling them the burners are completely rusted out. But anyway, I'll be talking to my staff about the schedule, and my mind just jumps from the trucks to Thursdays to the church grill, and then suddenly I'm going off about my boss’s tone of voice. He has this way of speaking that just... it really grates on you, you know? Very condescending. 

But the problem is, I’m supposed to be explaining the inventory, and the staff just stands there. They look at me like they completely can’t follow what I’m saying. It's like I lost them somewhere between the loading dock and the grill, and I don't really know how to fix it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech jumping between unrelated topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's tone) and notes that others cannot follow what they are saying, which is indicative of disorganized thinking and speech (derailment/tangentiality).

People won't buy it if the cardboard corners are all mashed in, they think the whole thing is ruined...

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices or other sounds when no one was around and nothing was making the noise?

It made me think about my brother's old truck—he had this Ford pickup back in the nineties, and a rock kicked up on the highway and completely shattered the windshield. We were driving down to the lake, and we had to pull over and tape a garbage bag over the window just to get back home. The wind was just whipping through the cab the whole way. I tried putting an anti-glare screen protector on my phone once, but I could never get the bubbles out. About six months, I guess. That's when I first noticed things getting a bit... jumbled, you know? Like I'd be out on the sales floor trying to explain something to the team, and I'd just stop. I'd lose the thread. It's been happening for about six months now. Which is right around the time they changed the vendor for our cardboard baler out back. 

The old baler was a workhorse, had this massive hydraulic press that never jammed. But they brought in this new eco-friendly model, and it's so finicky. You have to break down the boxes perfectly flat, or the sensor trips and the whole machine shuts down. We get these huge shipments of patio furniture in the spring—massive boxes, thick corrugated cardboard. And trying to get the seasonal crew to break those down right is like pulling teeth. I was showing this one kid how to score the corners with a box cutter so it folds flat, and my box cutter blade snapped right off. Just snapped. It flew across the receiving bay. Good thing I was wearing safety glasses. They make us wear these cheap plastic ones now, they fog up if you even look at them wrong. I tried wiping them with a microfiber cloth, but it just smeared the dust around... so yeah, about six months of the jumbled stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their thoughts getting 'jumbled' and losing the thread while speaking, and their response itself demonstrates tangentiality by drifting into a long, unrelated story about a cardboard baler and safety glasses.

My dad was always incredibly strict about how we treated the remote control when I was a kid. He had this big recliner, upholstered in that scratchy brown plaid fabric from the seventies, and the remote lived exactly on the right armrest. If you even moved it an inch, you were in serious trouble. He used to sit there and watch those old Westerns on Sunday afternoons, the ones with John Wayne, and he'd fall asleep halfway through... but anyway, no, I don't feel like things around me are sending me messages. turns.doctor_question: {"intent": "Screen for delusions of thought control, insertion, or broadcasting to assess for a second Criterion A symptom.", "question": "Have you ever felt like thoughts were being put into your head

No, I've never felt like thoughts were being put into my head. My thoughts are my own, you know? Just the usual stuff, mostly about work. It's hard to turn off the work brain when I get home. I'll be trying to relax, and suddenly I'm thinking about the scheduling matrix for next week. 

We use this automated scheduling software now, and it is an absolute disaster. It's supposed to optimize coverage based on foot traffic algorithms, but it always ends up scheduling three people for the Tuesday morning shift when the store is dead, and then leaves us with a skeleton crew on Saturday afternoon when everyone and their mother is trying to return things. The return desk gets so backed up. People bring back the craziest things. Last week, a lady tried to return a blender that she clearly bought like five years ago. It still had dried smoothie crust around the blades. She claimed she just bought it and it was defective, but she didn't have a receipt, obviously. We have a strict 30-day return policy, but if a customer complains loud enough, the store manager usually just caves and does a manual override. 

Manual overrides are a whole other headache because they mess up the inventory counts. I have to go in on the backend and adjust the stock levels, otherwise the system thinks we have three blenders when we actually have four, and then the automatic reordering system gets confused. I used to make my own smoothies for breakfast, actually. Spinach, banana, a little bit of almond milk. I bought this really nice insulated tumbler to take them to work, but I left it in the breakroom fridge over a long weekend and someone threw it out. Just tossed a perfectly good twenty-dollar tumbler because it had some green liquid in it. People have no respect for other people's property... but no, my thoughts are definitely my own. Nobody is putting them there.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering from work thoughts to scheduling software, a blender return, inventory counts, making smoothies, and a lost tumbler.

You try to use one of those cheap plastic ones and it just bends and snaps back at your fingers... but yeah, I still do my daily tasks just fine. No problems with motivation.

My grandfather had this old wooden rake that he used for decades. The handle was completely smooth from years of use, just perfectly worn down by his hands... but yeah, no head injuries for me. She said it smelled more like a "stagnant pond." I had to explain to her that we can't take back used liquid soap. She got so mad she threatened to call corporate. Corporate is useless, anyway. They just send down these automated email responses that don't actually address the issue. The emails always have this little animated graphic of a smiling shopping cart at the bottom, which just feels incredibly patronizing when you're trying to resolve a serious inventory discrepancy... but anyway, no, I'm not depressed. They always bring in these items that are clearly used, like a blender with smoothie still stuck to the blades, and they expect a full cash refund. Our policy clearly says store credit only without a receipt, and it has to be within thirty days. But they always argue. 

And the registers up there are the oldest ones in the store. The receipt printers constantly jam. You have to open the top, pull out the paper roll, and try to feed it back through this tiny little slot. The ink ribbons dry out, too, so the receipts print out super faint, and the customers complain they can't read them. I keep telling management we need thermal printers. Every other store uses thermal printers now. They're so much faster, and you don't have to deal with the ink. But of course, corporate won't approve the expense. They'd rather spend thousands of dollars on those stupid floor decals that peel up after a week. We put these giant arrows on the floor to direct traffic during the holiday rush, and the floor scrubber just tore them right up. Now there's just sticky residue everywhere, and the shopping carts get stuck on it... but anyway, no, I don't freeze up or go mute or anything. I'm always on the go.

turns.patient_response:
When I was younger? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I always talked fine. I was on the debate team in high school, actually. I could explain anything. 

Explaining things... that's the hardest part of my job right now, honestly. Trying to explain the new scheduling software to the part-timers. Corporate rolled out this app called "Kronos" or something, and everyone is supposed to check their shifts on their phones. But the app is constantly crashing. It won't let you log in if you're not connected to the store's Wi-Fi, but the store's Wi-Fi is a complete joke. It's supposed to be a secure network, but half the time it just drops the connection entirely, especially back in the stockroom where the walls are thick concrete. 

I had this one kid, Tyler, he's nineteen, works in electronics. He showed up three hours late on Tuesday because the app told him his shift started at noon instead of 9 AM. I tried to show him how to refresh the schedule page, but his phone is this ancient Android that barely holds a charge. The screen is cracked right down the middle, like a spiderweb. I don't know how he even reads anything on it. He said he dropped it in the parking lot last winter and just never got it fixed. Screen repairs are such a scam anyway. They charge you two hundred dollars just to replace the glass, and then a week later the touch sensor stops working. You're better off just buying a refurbished phone online. I bought a refurbished tablet a few years ago to read books on, but the battery life was terrible. I'd read for twenty minutes and it would drop to fifty percent... but yeah, no, I never had trouble talking or explaining things when I was a kid. I was always pretty articulate.
